title: Elodie and the Radiators
premise: After her mother's funeral, Tamsin Galloway returns to the shuttered family house to catalog a lifetime of silence, only to find a box of undelivered letters hidden behind her mother's wardrobe — all addressed to a woman named Elodie, and all returned unopened. As Tamsin reads twenty years of almost-confessions, she pieces together that Elodie was her mother's closest friend, possibly more, and that her own existence sits at the center of a choice her mother made to survive. The trail leads to a fading seaside boarding house called The Radiators, where Elodie's found family still gathers. In the final chapter, Tamsin delivers the last letter in person, speaks the sentence her mother never could, and chooses to keep the found family alive rather than let it die with the secret.
about_author: Cyrus Iversen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's unopened correspondence before turning to fiction. They write quietly devastating novels about inheritance, secrecy, and the families we assemble when the given ones fail.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV. Three days after the funeral, she begins cataloging her mother's house room by room, an act of avoidance disguised as duty. Every object resists explanation; her mother explained nothing in life either. Emotional beat: grief curdling into resentment as Tamsin realizes she is mourning not just a woman but a locked door.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV. Moving the wardrobe to repaint, she finds a cavity in the plaster holding a shoebox: forty-one letters, every one addressed to 'E. Marchetti' and stamped RETURN TO SENDER. The earliest dates from two years before Tamsin's birth. Emotional beat: vertigo — the discovery that her mother's silence had an addressee.

chapters.title: Dear E.,
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV, interwoven with excerpts of the first letters. Her mother's voice on the page is warmer, funnier, more alive than any version Tamsin knew. The letters reference shared rooms, shared cigarettes, a name for their flat's broken heating: 'the radiators.' Emotional beat: jealous wonder at a stranger who knew her mother better than she did.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin canvasses her mother's old neighborhood. An elderly shopkeeper recalls two young women inseparable until roughly 1989, then one gone overnight. He remembers the father — Tamsin's father — arriving like weather. Emotional beat: the first hard evidence that Elodie's disappearance coincides with Tamsin's conception.

chapters.title: The Unsent Reply
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV. Among the letters she finds a draft in her mother's handwriting, never mailed, beginning 'Elodie, I chose, and here is what it cost.' It stops mid-sentence. Tamsin reads it forty times. Emotional beat: recognition — her mother practiced the art of almost saying it too.

chapters.title: A Return Address That Isn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin traces the return stamp to a seaside town and finds The Radiators, a peeling boarding house still operating under a resident collective. A young caretaker, Dev, warns her the residents don't like questions about 'the old days.' Emotional beat: hope with a splinter in it.

chapters.title: The House That Keeps People
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He watches the stranger photograph the noticeboard and recognizes the surname from stories told after lights-out. He decides, against house custom, not to mention her visit yet. Emotional beat: loyalty tested by curiosity; the reader sees the found family from inside its defenses.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Version
chapters.summary: Tamsin gains entry by offering to fix a leaking radiator — literally. Longtime resident Mrs. Okonkwo tells a partial history: Elodie arrived broken-hearted in 1988 and built this household out of other people's leftovers. She goes silent when asked where Elodie is now. Emotional beat: warmth offered and withheld in the same breath.

chapters.title: Letters 12 Through 19
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV, reading by night. The middle letters chart the love affair in code — grocery lists, invented holidays, a plan to rent a cottage 'when it's safe.' Then letter 20 is missing entirely, a torn stub remaining. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into obsession; the missing letter becomes the book's gravitational center.

chapters.title: The Father's File
chapters.summary: Tamsin visits her estranged father in a care home, bringing one letter as bait. He reads it, weeps without explanation, and says only: 'Your mother paid so you wouldn't have to.' Emotional beat: the price of survival made flesh — he was complicit, or hostage, or both.

chapters.title: Dev Breaks the Rule
chapters.summary: Dev, POV. Unable to hold the secret, he tells Mrs. Okonkwo that Galloway's daughter has been asking around. The house convenes its nightly kitchen council. Some want Tamsin turned away; one voice argues she has a right to finish the sentence. Emotional beat: the found family fracturing over whether protection is kindness or theft.

chapters.title: Room 4
chapters.summary: Tamsin is finally allowed upstairs to Room 4, kept unchanged for decades: two toothbrushes, a ticket stub, a half-finished scarf. Mrs. Okonkwo admits Elodie is alive but refuses contact: 'She buried your mother thirty-five years ago. Let her rest.' Emotional beat: fury and understanding colliding in Tamsin's chest.

chapters.title: Letter 20, Reconstructed
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV. Cross-referencing the draft reply and the torn stub, she reconstructs letter 20's gist: her mother ended the relationship to marry, trading love for legitimacy and safety, believing she was protecting Elodie from scandal and herself from ruin. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of survival — someone always pays the difference.

chapters.title: Who Was Tamsin To Her?
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okonkwo reveals a detail: Elodie received one photo over the years — baby Tamsin — and kept it taped inside a cupboard door. Tamsin realizes she was not collateral damage; she was the reason Elodie stopped writing back. Emotional beat: identity shaken — she may be the wound, not just its heir.

chapters.title: The Tide Road
chapters.summary: Tamsin walks the coastal path Elodie walked daily, per Dev's reluctant tip-off, and finds her at the far end of the shingle: small, sharp-eyed, unmistakably the woman from the photographs. Elodie looks at her and says, 'You have her way of standing in doorways.' Emotional beat: the meeting the whole book has been walking toward, rendered almost wordless.

chapters.title: Two Cups, One Pot
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, the novel's only shift. Over tea she gives her account: the love, the ultimatum, the returned letters — returned because answering would have dragged her back into a life she couldn't survive twice. She does not absolve Tamsin's mother, and does not condemn her. Emotional beat: grief finally given a second chair to sit in.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Tamsin asks Elodie to read the unfinished draft aloud. Elodie completes the broken sentence in her mother's probable words — 'I chose you both, and lost you both, and I am sorry' — and hands it back. Emotional beat: climax; the untranslatable sentence translated at last, and it changes everything and fixes nothing.

chapters.title: What the House Decided
chapters.summary: Dev, POV. The kitchen council votes on whether Tamsin may stay through winter. Old grievances surface — everyone at The Radiators has traded something to be there. The vote passes narrowly. Emotional beat: found family as democracy, messy and conditional and real.

chapters.title: Wintering
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV. She stays, fixing radiators, learning the house's rituals, selling her mother's house to fund repairs. She writes a letter of her own and cannot finish it — then understands that finishing isn't the point; sending is. Emotional beat: the price of survival reframed as the cost of belonging, gladly paid.

chapters.title: Return to Sender, Opened
chapters.summary: Tamsin mails the completed draft — her mother's words plus her own postscript — to The Radiators, addressed to no one and everyone. The residents read it aloud at dinner. Emotional beat: catharsis; the silence finally delivered, twenty years late and exactly on time.

chapters.title: Elodie and the Radiators
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Spring. Elodie teaches Tamsin the scarf pattern left unfinished in Room 4; they argue about paint colors like people with a future. The house hums, warm for once. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — inheritance transformed from debt to gift.

chapters.title: The Last Entry in the Catalog
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV. She adds a final item to her inventory of the sold house: not an object but a sentence, written on a card and framed — the one her mother never said and she now says daily. Emotional beat: closure without erasure; some silences are inherited, and some can be answered.
